headline: Radio Call at 4 A.M., a Long Run South, and Bluefin Still Working the Jig
subhead: The eddy that's been holding warm water over Atlantis and Veatch hasn't budged, and the fleet running out of Montauk and Block Island is still cashing in on it.
body_markdown:
The radio traffic out of the Block Island and Montauk fleets this week has had a familiar rhythm: a captain calling in fish on the jig somewhere along the canyon edge, a course correction from the next boat back, and a third falling in behind on the same temperature line an hour later. That's not excitement talking — that's boats burning diesel efficiently, which is the whole game once you're running two, three, sometimes four hours each way to get to water that's actually holding fish. Nobody out here runs on hope. They run on what the last boat back to the dock told them, and this week that story hasn't changed much: the eddy sitting over Atlantis and Veatch is still there, still warm, and it's still stacking bluefin.

Stable high pressure held through the week, southwest wind in the 8-to-12 knot range most days, which is about as good as it gets for a long offshore run — flat enough riding out that a 32-to-38 footer can hold cruise speed without beating the crew up, which matters when the fuel math already has you thinking about the tank gauge before you clear the sea buoy. Boats out of Montauk are timing departures to be on the grounds by first light, working the water while it's calm, and turning for home before the afternoon sea breeze fills in. Out of Block Island and the Rhode Island ports, the run to Atlantis and Veatch eats a similar bite out of the day — long enough that most captains aren't making the trip on a maybe. They're going because the last two or three boats back confirmed fish, and that's exactly what's been happening.

The bluefin have been school-sized — footballs mostly, some pushing into the mid-range class — and they've been eating jigs cleanly along current edges where the warm water is folding against cooler stuff underneath. The go-to has been 180-gram-class jigs worked on a fast, erratic retrieve through the middle of the water column, with streaker-style natural bait rigs — ballyhoo or small squid strips dressed behind a skirted head — picking up fish that won't commit to straight metal. We flagged this a few days back, that the jig bite would hold as long as the eddy structure stayed in place, and it has. Same water, same pattern, same 180-gram jigs still doing the damage off Atlantis and Veatch. That's not a coincidence — warm-core eddies like this one don't dissolve on a schedule, they get pushed or pulled apart by something bigger, and nothing this week has come along to break it up.

Billfish have carried over from the same warm-water regime. White marlin have been showing along temperature breaks and weed lines on the troll, mixed in with the tuna spread more than targeted outright — a fish here, a fish there, not a bonanza, but enough that boats running dredge and daisy chain spreads through Hydrographer and Oceanographer have had shots. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure that's holding bait, which out here usually means a weed line or a piece of debris that's collected juvenile fish underneath it — nothing consistent enough to plan a whole trip around, but worth a look if you cross one on the troll and have a spinning rod rigged with a small bucktail or a chunk of squid ready to pitch.

What's kept this going is the moon building toward full, which has sharpened the current on the edges without blowing the structure apart. A stronger tide means bait gets pushed and pinned against the temperature break instead of drifting loose through it, and that's when the bluefin show up in numbers instead of ones and twos. It's the same logic that's been tightening bite windows closer to shore — Block Island and Point Judith should start seeing their first bonito of the season any day now as bait pulls tight along the beaches — but offshore, the effect is on the eddy itself: tighter current, tighter bait, better jig bite.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern holds if the weather does. Southwest wind in that same comfortable range should keep the ride manageable through the weekend, and there's no sign yet of the eddy sliding off Atlantis or losing its warm core. If that holds, the smart move is the same one the fleet's already making — run early, work the edges where the color changes from blue to green-blue, and stick with the 180-gram jigs until something tells you to switch. Where this gets interesting is the 72-hour window. Overnight temperatures up in the northern reaches are starting to nudge down a notch, which won't touch the canyons directly but is usually the first sign the season's turning behind the scenes. The warm-water regime offshore should hold through that window regardless — these eddies don't answer to a calendar the way the inshore water does — but it's worth watching whether that cooling trend starts pulling the whole system south and east over the next week or two. For now, if you've got the fuel and the weather window, Atlantis and Veatch are still paying off. Just don't leave the dock without knowing exactly how much diesel it takes to get home.
